title: What My First Job Taught Me
script: Narrator: [warmly] My first job was at a small shop near my house. I was twenty years old, and I knew almost nothing about working life.
Narrator: On my first day, I was so nervous that I dropped a box of cups in front of a customer. My face turned completely red.
Narrator: [honestly] The manager just laughed a little and said, everyone breaks something on their first day, don't worry about it.
Narrator: That small moment taught me something important. Mistakes are normal, and people usually remember how you handle them, not the mistake itself.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I worked there for two years, folding clothes, using the cash register, and helping customers find what they needed.
Narrator: The pay was small, and the hours were long. Some days I stood for eight hours straight without a real break.
Narrator: [carefully] But I also learned things school never taught me, like how to stay calm when a customer is angry, and how to work as a team.
Narrator: My coworker Sinta became a close friend during that time. We covered each other's shifts and shared lunch almost every day.
Narrator: [reflective] One day, a customer shouted at me because we didn't have the size she wanted. I wanted to cry, but I stayed polite instead.
Narrator: Later, my manager told me she was proud of how I handled it. That comment meant more to me than any paycheck.
Narrator: [practically] I eventually left that job for something better, but I still think about it often, especially on hard days at my current job.
Narrator: It taught me patience, and it taught me that every job, even a small one, can teach you something worth keeping.
Narrator: [calmly] Now, when I train new employees, I try to be as patient as my first manager was with me.
Narrator: I remember how scared I felt on that first day, and I try to make new people feel less alone.
Narrator: [encouraging] Income matters, and a first job can also teach how we respond when work becomes difficult.
